source.citation: Owens ACS, Meyer-Rochow VB, Yang E-C (2018). Short- and mid-wavelength artificial light influences the flash signals of Aquatica ficta fireflies (Coleoptera: Lampyridae). PLoS ONE 13(2): e0191576

scope: Reported results of the paper only; no re-analysis of the raw recordings (human decision, AI_LOG round 4a). Values are copied as printed.

label_notes.documented: Owens ACS, Meyer-Rochow VB, Yang E-C (2018). Short- and mid-wavelength artificial light influences the flash signals of Aquatica ficta fireflies (Coleoptera: Lampyridae). PLoS ONE 13(2): e0191576, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0191576; page given per item.
label_notes.inferred: text_vs_table1: rule in pipeline/impacts/08_owens2018.py docstring; inputs = text_p_values and table1.

units.flash_intensity: counts (spectrometer, average relative intensity 565-569 nm per 100 ms; average peak intensity per 1 min recording, first 15 s omitted)
units.ratio_to_dark: Table 1 "degree of change relative to dark": mean divided by the 1 min dark base value (5420 counts; 43.167 peaks/min)
units.sd: standard deviation, as printed ("x̄ ± SD" in the Table 1 header); Fig 2 caption: N = 6
units.p: Table 1 "p-value" column, as printed. The table does not name the test; the Methods (p. 4) compare intensity and frequency per wavelength with GLMMs, dim and bright analysed separately

table1.caption: Table 1. Average peak intensity and frequency of light signals produced by A. ficta under exposure to varying wavelengths and intensities of ambient light.
table1.columns_printed: λ (nm) | flash intensity x̄ ± SD (counts) | degree of change relative to dark (bright/dark) | p-value | flash frequency x̄ ± SD (peaks/min) | degree of change relative to dark (bright/dark) | p-value

text_vs_table1.rule: same exposure, measure, wavelength; "=" agrees if equal, "<" agrees if the Table 1 p is below the bound

species.quote: Three male A. fictafireflies were collected three times from Yongjian Eco Park

alarm_flash.label: documented

recorded_band.label: documented

sampling.quote: Averages were calculated and saved every 100 ms.
sampling.label: documented

leds.label: documented

exposure_protocol.label: documented

dim_bright_flux.quote: ranging from 0.107 ±0.02 μmol m-2 s-1 and from 1.075 ±0.212 μmol m-2 s-1 for dim and bright exposures, respectively
dim_bright_flux.label: documented

dim_bright_lux.label: documented

sample.quote: Eight sets of data were collected from eight A. fictamales on the evenings of May 5–9 and May 12–14, 2016 (S2 Fig; one male died before it could be tested). Of these, two recordings (May 5 and May 13) were disregarded
sample.label: documented

n_analysed.quote: Flash intensity and frequency data from six individuals
n_analysed.label: documented

noise_threshold.quote: Measurements 200 counts were excluded as noise
noise_threshold.label: documented
noise_threshold.as_printed: Measurements ≤ 200 counts were excluded as noise

adaptation.quote: The first 15 s of each recording was defined as the “adapta- tion period”
adaptation.label: documented

model.quote: Average flash intensity and frequency under each wavelength of exposure was compared using generalized linear mixed models (GLMM)
model.label: documented

baseline_fig2.quote: Base values for average flash intensity (5420 counts) and flash frequency (43.167 peaks/min) obtained from 1 min dark recordings
baseline_fig2.label: documented

fig2_error_bars.quote: Change in average (±1 SE) flash intensity (A) and frequency (B)
fig2_error_bars.label: documented

abstract_short_mid.quote: When exposed to wavelengths at or below 533 nm, males emitted brighter signals with decreased frequency.
abstract_short_mid.label: documented

abstract_long.quote: long wavelength ambient light ( 597 nm) did not affect signal morphology
abstract_long.label: documented
abstract_long.as_printed: long wavelength ambient light (≥ 597 nm) did not affect signal morphology

exposure_order_models.quote: Exposure order explained a large amount of observed variation in flash frequency. However, it did not have an observable impact on flash intensity and was subsequently dropped from that set of models.
exposure_order_models.label: documented

frequency_decline_cause.quote: The decline is due to increases in interpulse interval [58] and, to a lesser extent, flash duration (S2 Table)
frequency_decline_cause.label: documented

pauses.quote: sporadic periods without flashing were more common under illumination, sometimes continuing for 10 or more seconds
pauses.label: documented

intensity_increase.quote: average peak inten- sity of flash signals significantly increased, sometimes more than 100%, when individuals were exposed to dim intensities of short- and mid-wavelength light
intensity_increase.label: documented

ceased_signalling.quote: under bright short- and mid-wavelength illumination, three of six males ceased signaling entirely
ceased_signalling.label: documented

long_wavelength_no_effect.quote: neither dim nor bright intensities of long wavelength ( 597 nm) illumination had a signifi- cant effect on flash intensity or frequency (p 0.3 in all instances; Fig 2)
long_wavelength_no_effect.label: documented
long_wavelength_no_effect.as_printed: neither dim nor bright intensities of long wavelength (≥ 597 nm) illumination had a signifi- cant effect on flash intensity or frequency (p ≥ 0.3 in all instances; Fig 2)

exposure_order_anova.quote: number of previous exposures had a significant negative effect on flash frequency (1×: p <0.0001, χ2 = 15.205; 10×: p = 0.0012, χ2 = 14.668), but not flash intensity (p = 1.0 and χ2 = 0 in both 1×and 10×models)
exposure_order_anova.label: documented

intensity_frequency_correlation.quote: this potentially beneficial behavior may require some decrease in average flash frequency [correlation coefficient: -0.9655009 (1×), -0.8027756 (10×)]
intensity_frequency_correlation.label: documented

half_stopped_bright.quote: half of the A. fictaspecimens stopped flashing under bright (10×) exposures
half_stopped_bright.label: documented

red_not_responsive.quote: Our results suggest that A. fictais not visually responsive to red wavelengths.
red_not_responsive.label: documented

recommendation.quote: Our results suggest artificial light sources emitting the majority of their light in wavelengths 597 nm, including a range of yellow to red wavelengths visible to humans, would be most suitable for A. fictahabitats.
recommendation.label: documented
recommendation.as_printed: Our results suggest artificial light sources emitting the majority of their light in wavelengths ≥ 597 nm, including a range of yellow to red wavelengths visible to humans, would be most suitable for A. fictahabitats.

not_reported: Per-male values: the paper gives means ± SD (Table 1), not the individual values.
Fig 1 (p. 5): example recordings of two males (counts per 100 ms over 4 min; dark / dim / bright 533 nm); drawn only, not digitised (not requested).
Fig 2 means and SE: drawn only (bars, ±1 SE); no numbers in the text. Not digitised (not requested).
S1 Table (exposure sequence, μW/cm2), S2 Table (flash duration, interpulse interval), S1 Text, S1-S2 Fig: separate supplementary files, not in this PDF and not obtained.
Bold p-values in Table 1: the rendered page shows some p-values in bold; the text layer carries no bold and the paper does not state what bold means. Not recorded.
What "±" means for the dim/bright photon flux (SD or other) is not stated.
Table 1 headers read "degree of change relative to dark (bright/dark)" in both the dim and the bright block, as printed.
The correlation coefficients (p. 8) do not say which correlation statistic or which variables per se; kept as the quote.
